newsitem.title: GERMANY: EMU delay talk gains currency after Waigel remarks.
newsitem.headline: EMU delay talk gains currency after Waigel remarks.

text.p: Talk that Europe's single currency project might be delayed grew on Monday as German Finance Minister Theo Waigel said meeting the economic targets for membership took precedence over the timetable and opposition leaders warned that Bonn had no hope of qualifying on time.

Waigel, struggling to calm German fears that the planned single currency, the euro, would not be as stable as the mark, told the Bild newspaper: "There won't be any soft euro with me. The important thing is criteria have precedence over timetable."
"We shall in the next nine months do all we can to fulfil the Maastricht stability criteria."

While Waigel has said this several times before, economists called the remarks significant as they came at a time of mounting doubt about Germany's ability to qualify for European economic and monetary union (EMU).

The comments revived general uncertainty about EMU and helped boost the mark against the Spanish peseta and Italian lira, which rose above 1,000 lire to the mark for the first time in two weeks. That prompted mark sales by the central banks of Italy and Spain.

The budget spokesman for the opposition Social Democrats (SPD), Karl Diller, said Bonn did not stand a chance of meeting the criteria in time for the January 1, 1999 launch date of EMU because spending was "out of control."

Citing finance ministry data, Diller said the federal deficit for January and February already amounted to 34.8 billion marks ($20.5 billion), two thirds of the level of 53.3 billion budgeted for the full year.
"Chancellor (Helmut Kohl) should come clean on how things are to proceed with Europe. Under this government, Germany stands no chance of meeting the Maastricht goal," Diller said.

The relentless rise in unemployment has cast doubt on Germany's ability to cut its budget deficit below the ceiling of three percent of gross domestic product (GDP) set by the Maastricht Treaty requirements for joining EMU.
The government's official deficit forecast for 1997, the year on which EMU hopefuls will be judged, is 2.9 percent, down from 3.8 percent last year.

But many private economists and several Bundesbank officials have said they doubt this will be possible in view of the squeeze on tax revenues and rise in benefit payments caused by unemployment rising to post-World War Two records this year.

Waigel's comments came after his finance ministry at the weekend denied a report in Der Spiegel news magazine that internal government calculations showed the budget deficit climbing as high as 4.15 percent of GDP in 1997.

Economists said his remarks contrasted with the stance taken by Kohl who has so far avoided setting a priority between the timetable and the criteria but will probably be unable to avoid doing so for much longer.
Kohl has consistently said Germany will meet the criteria and that monetary union will start on time.
Thomas Mayer, senior economist at Goldman Sachs, said Kohl was likely to wait until mid-year, when a clearer picture of Germany's EMU chances emerge, before setting a priority.
"Then he will have to show his colours and state that the criteria are more important than the timetable. If Kohl says that, markets will take this as a strong hint that a delay is on the cards."

Gerhard Schroeder, premier of the state of Lower Saxony and tipped as SPD contender for the chancellorship in the 1998 general election, said EMU should be delayed as Germany could not qualify without creative accounting.
Schroeder told Britain's Financial Times in an interview he did not believe a delay would damage Europe in the long run.
Meanwhile, German Economics Minister Guenter Rexrodt said he was certain Germany would qualify on time, a view echoed by the German Banking Federation which predicted EMU would go ahead on schedule.
($ = 1.695 German Marks)
